NOVEL-AND-FEASIBLE IDEATION:

STEP 1 — INVENT THE OBSERVABLE:
Standard practice tracks terminal voltage and specific gravity as indicators of state of charge and overall health. My observable is the thermal dissipation coefficient (α) derived from the temperature coefficient of resistance, which directly correlates with grid cross-section reduction due to corrosion.

STEP 2 — MAKE THE IMPLEMENTATION BORING:
The observable can be computed from existing temperature sensors and voltage/current measurements using standard resistance calculation and thermal analysis principles, requiring only software modification to existing battery monitoring systems.

NOVELTY STATEMENT:
Standard practice tracks terminal voltage and specific gravity as bulk indicators of charge state and overall battery health. My observable, the thermal dissipation coefficient (α), represents a departure by quantifying the relationship between temperature rise and current flow, which directly reflects the increasing internal resistance from grid cross-section reduction. This connects to failure physics through the Joule heating effect (P = I²R), where increasing R from corrosion raises thermal dissipation at constant current.

PHYSICS CHECK:
The governing physical relation is α = ΔT/(I²R), where ΔT is temperature rise above ambient, I is current, and R is internal resistance. For a typical VRLA battery with 1 mΩ internal resistance at 10A discharge, ΔT would be approximately 0.1°C, giving α ≈ 1000°C/A². This magnitude is detectable with standard ±0.5°C temperature sensors and ±1% current measurement.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL:
Components:
- Existing temperature sensors (already installed on battery terminals)
- Existing current sensors (shunt or Hall-effect, already in place)
- Existing voltage measurement system
- Software modification to existing battery management system

Procedure:
1. Measure steady-state temperature rise (ΔT) during float charge at 2.27V/cell
2. Measure float current (I)
3. Calculate internal resistance: R = (V_terminal - V_open_circuit)/I
4. Calculate thermal dissipation coefficient: α = ΔT/(I²R)
5. Implement trending algorithm to track α over time

All components are standard and already installed. Only software development is required, using conventional signal processing and trending algorithms.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY):
- Installability: SAME - uses existing sensors, no additional hardware
- Operability: SAME - integrates with existing monitoring systems
- Maintenance: SAME - no additional maintenance requirements
- Cost class: SAME - only software development cost, no additional hardware

The approach imposes the same deployment burden as standard practice while providing a novel, physics-based indicator of grid corrosion that standard practice cannot detect.

EXECUTABLE TEST:
Protocol:
1. Install test batteries with 2% antimony content in float service at 2.27V/cell
2. Monitor thermal dissipation coefficient (α) continuously
3. Record α monthly alongside standard measurements
4. Continue testing until capacity falls below 80% of rated value

Pass/fail threshold: α increase greater than 10% per year indicates unacceptable grid corrosion rate

Duration: 15 years or until capacity falls below service threshold

Kill criterion: If α increases by more than 10% in any 12-month period, the design is falsified as failing to meet the 15-year service life requirement under the stated constraint.
